notes.meaning: A widow whose late husband was part of a company of prophets cries out to Elisha for help. Under the law of Moses, an unpaid lender had the legal right to take a debtor's children as servants to work off a debt. The woman reminds Elisha that her husband faithfully feared the Lord and did not bring this debt upon them through reckless living. God cares deeply about the cries of families facing hardship.

Elisha asks how he can help and what resources she still has in her home. She replies that she owns nothing of value except a small flask of olive oil, probably kept for anointing. God often begins his work of providing for us by using the small, humble things we already have.

Elisha tells the widow to borrow empty jars and pots from all her neighbors and not to collect just a few. Gathering empty containers from neighbors tested her faith, since she had to act before seeing any miracle. Her willingness to collect many jars showed she expected the Lord to do something great.

The prophet instructs her to go inside her home with her sons and shut the door behind them. Keeping the door closed gave the family privacy, prevented a public spectacle, and allowed them to focus on God in quiet prayer. She was to pour oil into each borrowed jar until it was completely full.

The widow follows Elisha's instructions and closes the door behind herself and her sons. Her sons keep bringing empty jars to her, and she steadily pours oil from her small flask into them. God multiplied the oil through this simple act of shared family obedience.

The oil continues to flow as long as there is an empty jar ready to receive it. Once her son tells her that no more jars are left, the flow of oil suddenly stops. God's grace never runs dry on its own; it pours out freely to meet every open and needy heart.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some prosperity teachers claim this event shows that God's financial supply is limited only by how much seed money or financial faith a believer puts forward.

notes.meaning: Instead of selling the oil immediately, the woman goes back to Elisha to ask what she should do with God's gift. He tells her to sell the oil, pay her debt honestly, and use the remaining money to provide for herself and her sons. God not only solved her immediate crisis but also provided for her future needs.

Elisha travels to Shunem, a town in northern Israel, where a wealthy and respected woman urges him to eat a meal at her house. After this warm welcome, Elisha makes it a habit to stop and eat there whenever his travels bring him through the area. Her generous hospitality provided a dependable place of rest for God's traveling servant.

After observing Elisha over time, the woman recognizes that he is not just an ordinary traveler, but a true prophet dedicated to the Lord. His holy character and upright life proved that he belonged completely to God. She talks with her husband to plan a more permanent way to care for him.

She asks her husband to prepare a small walled room on the roof with basic furniture: a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp. This gave Elisha a quiet place away from household noise where he could rest, study, and pray. She expected nothing in return, simply wishing to meet the everyday needs of God's prophet.
Elisha arrives in Shunem and goes up to the quiet upper room prepared for him to lie down and rest. The woman's thoughtfulness gave him a peaceful refuge after long ministry travels across Israel.

Elisha tells his servant Gehazi to call their hostess so he can speak with her. Gehazi calls her, and she comes and stands respectfully before the prophet. Her willingness to come shows her continued reverence for the man of God.

Elisha offers to speak to the king or the army commander on her behalf to help her family, since the prophet had strong standing at court. She humbly declines, explaining that she lives safely and happily among her own people. She cared for God's prophet out of pure kindness, not to gain royal favors or advance in society.

After the woman leaves the room, Elisha asks Gehazi what kind of kindness they might still show her. Gehazi points out that she has no son and her husband is elderly, making children unlikely. In ancient Israel, childlessness brought deep personal grief and social reproach.
Elisha tells Gehazi to summon the woman once more. When she returns, she pauses and stands modestly in the doorway of the room.

Elisha announces that at the same time the next year, she will hold a baby boy in her arms. Overwhelmed by the news, she begs the prophet not to deceive her with false hope. Her reaction came from the shock of a joy she had long given up hoping for, much like Sarah in the book of Genesis.

God honors the word spoken by Elisha, and the woman becomes pregnant. Exactly one year later, she gives birth to a son, just as the prophet had promised. God rewarded her quiet devotion and hospitality with the gift of new life.
The boy grows into childhood and goes out one day to the fields to visit his father during the harvest. His father was working alongside the reapers as they gathered grain.

While in the fields, the young boy suddenly cries out in agony about intense pain in his head. In the heat of the harvest season, he likely suffered a severe sunstroke. Not realizing how dangerous the illness was, his father tells a servant to carry the boy home to his mother.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern commentators suggest that rather than a common sunstroke, the boy suffered a sudden brain aneurysm.

notes.meaning: The servant carries the suffering child into the home and hands him to his mother. She cradles the boy on her lap, trying to comfort him, until he dies at noon. Even the deepest love and care of a mother could not keep this promised child alive.

The grieving mother carries her dead son up to the prophet's room and lays his body on Elisha's bed, then shuts the door behind her. By keeping the death private, she prevents an immediate burial and acts out of faith that God can restore him. Her actions show confidence that Elisha, like Elijah before him, could bring her child back to life.

She asks her husband for a servant and a donkey so she can ride urgently to find the prophet and return home quickly. She deliberately keeps the child's death a secret from her husband so she can seek the man of God without delay. Her steady composure reveals a mother who refused to give in to despair.
